question: State the definition of a prime number and give the first five primes.
Using only the definition from Q1, prove that 2 is the only even prime.
Given Q1–Q2, explain why every integer greater than 2 that is not prime must have a prime factor ≤ its square root.
Apply the result of Q3 to test whether 91 is prime; show the work.
State the Euclidean algorithm for computing gcd(a,b).
Using the algorithm from Q5, compute gcd(252,105) and list every remainder.
From the remainders in Q6, express gcd(252,105) as an integer linear combination of 252 and 105 (Bézout coefficients).
Given Q5–Q7, prove that if d divides a and d divides b then d divides any integer linear combination of a and b.
State the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.
Using Q9, prove that if a prime p divides the product ab then p divides a or p divides b.
Apply Q10 to show that √2 is irrational.
Given Q9–Q11, generalize the argument to prove that √p is irrational for any prime p.
Define a mathematical function f:A→B and the notions injective, surjective, and bijective.
Using Q13, prove that a function f:A→B is bijective if and only if it has an inverse function.
Give an explicit bijection between the set of integers ℤ and the set of even integers.
Given Q13–Q15, prove that the set of rational numbers ℚ is countable.
State the definition of a limit of a sequence: lim n→∞ a_n = L.
Using the ε-N definition from Q17, prove that lim n→∞ (1/n) = 0.
Prove that the limit of a sum is the sum of the limits, assuming both limits exist.
Given Q17–Q19, prove that lim n→∞ (n/(n+1)) = 1.
State the definition of a derivative of a function f at a point a.
Using the definition from Q21, compute f'(x) for f(x)=x² from first principles.
Prove the product rule (fg)' = f'g + fg' using the definition of derivative.
Given Q21–Q23, derive the power rule for positive integers: (x^n)' = n x^{n-1}.
State the Intermediate Value Theorem.
Using Q25, prove that every odd-degree polynomial with real coefficients has at least one real root.
State the Mean Value Theorem.
Given Q25–Q27, prove that if f'(x)=0 for all x in an interval then f is constant on that interval.
Define a vector space over the real numbers and give the axioms.
Using Q29, prove that the zero vector is unique.
Define linear independence of a set of vectors.
Given Q29–Q31, prove that any set of more than n vectors in ℝ^n is linearly dependent.
State the rank-nullity theorem.
Apply Q33 to a linear map T:ℝ³→ℝ² whose kernel has dimension 1; what is the dimension of the image?
Define an eigenvalue and eigenvector of a square matrix.
Using Q35, compute the eigenvalues of the matrix [[2,1],[1,2]].
Prove that eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent.
Given Q35–Q37, diagonalize the matrix from Q36 if possible and show the steps.
State Newton’s second law and the definition of work done by a force.
Using Q39, derive the work–energy theorem for a particle under a constant force.
Define kinetic energy and potential energy for a conservative force.
Given Q39–Q41, prove that total mechanical energy is conserved when only conservative forces act.
State the first law of thermodynamics.
Using Q43, explain why a perpetual-motion machine of the first kind is impossible.
State the second law of thermodynamics in terms of entropy.
Given Q43–Q45, explain why a perpetual-motion machine of the second kind is impossible.
Define electric field and electric potential due to a point charge.
Using Q47, derive the relationship E = −∇V in electrostatics.
State Gauss’s law for electricity.
Given Q47–Q49, use Gauss’s law to find the electric field outside a uniformly charged sphere.
State the Schrödinger equation for a single particle in one dimension.
Using Q51, write the time-independent Schrödinger equation and explain the meaning of the energy eigenvalue.
Solve the particle-in-a-box problem: infinite walls at x=0 and x=L; give the energy levels.
Given Q51–Q53, explain why the energy of a free particle in a box cannot be zero.
Define a formal proposition and the connectives ¬, ∧, ∨, →.
Using Q55, construct the truth table for (P → Q) ∧ (Q → R) → (P → R).
Prove that the formula in Q56 is a tautology.
Given Q55–Q57, prove that modus ponens is a valid rule of inference.
Define a first-order language with quantifiers ∀ and ∃.
Using Q59, formalize the statement ‘every natural number has a successor’.
State the principle of mathematical induction.
Given Q59–Q61, prove by induction that the sum of the first n positive integers is n(n+1)/2.
Define a graph (simple, undirected) and the notions of path, cycle, and connectedness.
Using Q63, prove that a tree with n vertices has exactly n−1 edges.
State Euler’s formula for planar graphs: v − e + f = 2.
Given Q63–Q65, prove that K₅ is not planar.
Define a probability space (Ω, F, P) and the axioms of probability.
Using Q67, prove that P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).
Define conditional probability and state Bayes’ theorem.
Given Q67–Q69, solve: a test is 99% accurate for a disease that occurs in 0.1% of the population; what is the probability a person who tests positive actually has the disease?
Define expected value of a discrete random variable.
Using Q71, compute the expected value of a fair six-sided die.
Prove linearity of expectation: E[X+Y] = E[X] + E[Y] even when X and Y are dependent.
Given Q71–Q73, compute the expected number of fixed points of a random permutation of n elements.
State the central limit theorem (qualitative form).
Using Q75, explain why the sample mean of i.i.d. random variables becomes approximately normal for large n.
Define a group and give the group axioms.
Using Q77, prove that the identity element of a group is unique.
Prove that every element of a group has a unique inverse.
Given Q77–Q79, show that (ℤ/nℤ, +) is a group and identify the inverse of k.
Define a ring and an integral domain.
Using Q81, prove that a finite integral domain is a field.
State Fermat’s Little Theorem.
Given Q81–Q83, prove Fermat’s Little Theorem using the fact that (ℤ/pℤ)* is a multiplicative group.
Define a metric space and an open ball.
Using Q85, prove that an open ball is an open set.
Define a continuous function between metric spaces via open sets.
Given Q85–Q87, prove that the composition of continuous functions is continuous.
State the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem.
Using Q89, prove that a continuous function on a closed bounded interval attains its maximum and minimum.
Define a Cauchy sequence in a metric space.
Given Q89–Q91, prove that a metric space is complete if every Cauchy sequence converges.
State the completeness of the real numbers as an axiom (least-upper-bound property).
Using Q93, prove that every Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges.
Define the notion of a logical consequence: a set of premises Γ entails a formula φ.
Using Q95, prove that if Γ entails φ and Γ entails (φ → ψ) then Γ entails ψ.
State the soundness theorem for classical propositional logic.
Given Q95–Q97, explain why a sound proof system can never derive a contradiction from consistent premises.
State Gödel’s first incompleteness theorem (informal version).

Given the entire chain Q1–Q99, identify which results rely only on finitary combinatorial reasoning and which require a form of completeness or infinitary assumption, and explain how that distinction would affect a cached-pathway verification system that must decide whether a derived claim is still valid after a premise is withdrawn.
